text: Then five years passed.
And in May 2026, the Illinois Answers Project went and checked what the ordinance had actually delivered.
The results were thin.
Of the 52 reserved lots, exactly one project had been finished, a single building of 58 units.
The tenant right of first refusal, the one tool meant to let renters buy before a sale, had generated zero notices in five years.
A home-repair grant program reached just 36 longtime homeowners, with grants of up to 20,000 dollars each.

And roughly 2 million dollars set aside to preserve and rehab housing sat completely unspent, in part because almost no one applied and no one inside the city was clearly assigned to push the money out the door.
The protections were real on paper.
On the ground, they barely slowed the wave.
The people the ordinance was written to keep in place were leaving while the money it promised them sat in an account.
To understand why a doubling of home prices lands so hard in a place like Woodlawn, you have to know how Black families in Chicago came to own homes in the first place.
For decades, redlining and racial covenants shut them out of ordinary bank mortgages.
The loans that built white wealth in the suburbs were simply not on offer.
So when Black families finally bought, on the South and West Sides, a huge share of them bought on contract.
A contract sale looked like a mortgage and worked nothing like one.
A speculator would buy a house cheap from a fleeing white owner, then turn around and sell it to a Black family at a steep markup, on terms the family had no power to refuse.
The seller kept the deed until the very last payment was made, years down the line.
The buyer built no equity along the way, and got none of the protections a real mortgage carried.
And miss a single payment, even one, and the seller could evict and keep everything already paid, then sell the same house to the next family and start the whole cycle again.
Families took in boarders and worked second jobs just to make the monthly number.
